title: CDD: centred double decrease
subtitle: Removing two stitches at once with a centred, symmetrical decrease.
excerpt: The centred double decrease (CDD) slips two stitches together knitwise, knits the next stitch, then passes the two slipped stitches over. Three stitches become one, and the decrease leans neither left nor right, making it the standard choice for symmetrical shaping at the peak of a V-neckline or the point of a lace motif.
sourceNotes: The centred double decrease is documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) and Weldon's Practical Knitter lace sections. Modern UK pattern writing convention abbreviates it CDD; equivalent to the US sl2-k1-p2sso.
heroPrompt: Close-up of a symmetrical lace motif in which a centred double decrease forms the central point of a diamond, the decrease column running perfectly vertical.

glossaryTerms.definition: A decrease that removes two stitches by slipping two together knitwise, knitting one, then passing the two slipped stitches over the knitted stitch. The decrease leans neither left nor right and is used for symmetrical shaping.
Any decrease that removes two stitches in one operation, reducing a stitch count by two. Examples include CDD (centred), sk2p (left-leaning), and k3tog (right-leaning).

content.text: reduces three stitches to one in a single operation. Unlike a right-leaning k3tog or a left-leaning sk2p, the CDD sits vertically: the central stitch of the three lies on top of the finished decrease stitch, so the column runs straight up the fabric without pulling to either side. It is the correct decrease for the apex of a V-neckline, the peak of a lace diamond, and the tip of a Faroese shawl point. Difficulty: intermediate.
Any yarn and needles appropriate for the project
A practice swatch of at least 15 stitches in stocking stitch to see the result clearly
Work to the point where the decrease is to be placed.

Insert the right needle into the first two stitches simultaneously as if to knit two together (entering both stitches at once from left to right). Slip them both onto the right needle together without working them. This is the key move: slipping the two stitches knitwise keeps them oriented correctly for the finish.
Knit the next stitch (the third of the three) in the normal way.
Insert the left needle tip from left to right through the fronts of the two slipped stitches on the right needle. Pass both slipped stitches over the knitted stitch and off the right needle.
One stitch remains where three existed. The central stitch of the original three now sits on top.

attrs.title: CDD compared to sk2p
attrs.body: The sk2p (slip 1 knitwise, k2tog, pass slipped stitch over) is also a double decrease, but it leans slightly to the left. The CDD is truly centred because it slips the two leftmost stitches together, making the middle stitch (the one between them) sit on top. In lace, use CDD when the pattern chart shows a vertical line; use sk2p or k3tog when the chart shows a leaning line.

content.text: CDD appears at the centre of symmetrical shaping: the apex of a V-neckline where decreases on both sides meet, the top of a lace diamond or triangle motif, the centre of a mitre-square corner, and any pattern note that specifies 'work a centred double decrease' or 'cdd'. It pairs with yarn overs in lace to maintain stitch count while shaping the motif outline.

items.symptom: The decrease leans to the left rather than sitting straight
items.cause: The two stitches were slipped purlwise rather than knitwise
items.fix: Slip both stitches together by entering the needle from left to right (as if to k2tog), not from right to left (as if to p2tog). Knitwise entry keeps them oriented correctly.

items.symptom: The central stitch does not sit on top and the decrease looks like sk2p
items.cause: Only one stitch was slipped, or the two slips were done separately
items.fix: Slip the two stitches simultaneously by entering both at once with the right needle tip. Slipping them separately changes the orientation of each stitch.

items.symptom: A hole appears below the decrease
items.cause: The stitches were not snugged up before passing over
items.fix: After knitting the centre stitch, hold the work firm and pass the two slipped stitches over in one smooth motion without allowing extra yarn to feed in.
